But knowledge may also arrive suddenly in the heart, as though placed there, without the person's deliberate effort (ijtihad).

That sudden gift may come without any awareness or vision of the being who gives it. This is inspiration (ilham), the way the Imams—heirs of the Prophet—and God's spiritually initiated friends (awliya) receive knowledge. At other times, the appearance of knowledge within the heart is accompanied by seeing or hearing the angel who brings it, either in a dream or while awake.

The teaching thus takes account of several different states of awareness. At its highest level comes divine communication through the angel (wahy), reserved for the great prophets entrusted with revealing a new sacred law (sharia). The entire account of prophecy will depend on these distinctions.

Mulla Sadra explains how knowledge reaches the heart by describing the angel's part in it. Gabriel, or the Active Intellect, is the being the Qur'an refers to as the Pen (al-Qalam, 68:1): the one “through whom God writes on the tablets of hearts.” This angel is a sacred spiritual being, made of light. He stands between God and human beings so that knowledge can become present in their hearts.
As Mulla Sadra puts it, the angel plays this part “just as the pen stands between a writer and the surface—paper or tablet—on which the written marks appear.”

The relation between this luminous being and the things we can know is therefore like the relation between light and the things we can see. The comparison works for both kinds of sight: our outward vision (basar al-zahir) and our inward vision (basirat al-batin).

Our eyes see when sunlight makes things visible. The heart, which is the seat of understanding, knows when the angel—the Pen, the Active Intellect—sheds its light. The heart is like the eye in another respect, too: it can be blind.
But there could hardly be a view of knowledge further removed from the belief that ultimate reality is beyond our knowing. This is a theory that grew out of the philosophy of Avicenna.
The image that keeps returning is that of two mirrors. In the first is the Preserved Tablet (Lawh mahfuz), bearing everything God has inscribed upon it.

The second is the human heart. Divine knowledge appears in the heart as the image in one mirror may be reflected into another. At first, a veil separates them. Philosophers try to draw it aside through their own efforts.
But sometimes a breath of divine wind lifts the veil from the eye of the heart ('ayn al-qalb). That is what happens to those who receive inspiration.

So the philosopher's knowledge and inspired knowledge are not two completely different kinds of thing. Mulla Sadra insists that the angel of knowledge is also the angel of revelation. Inspiration differs from knowledge reached through effort not in what is known, not in where it is received—the heart—and not in its source—the angel, the Pen, the Active Intellect. The difference is how far the veil has been lifted, something human choice alone cannot bring about.

Whenever knowledge becomes real within our hearts, it does so through the angel (bi-wasitat al-mala'ika). This, Mulla Sadra says, is what the Qur'an means when it says: “It is not given to a human being that God should speak to him except through communication [by an angel, wahy], or from behind a veil. Or He sends a messenger who, by His permission, conveys whatever God wishes” (42:50–51).

We now have what we need to understand how the central idea of Twelver Shiism takes shape: the Imam as a spiritual guide. His position becomes clear once we distinguish the different kinds of prophets according to the ways they receive knowledge.
A long teaching attributed to the Sixth Imam, Ja'far al-Sadiq, and preserved in al-Kulayni's great collection, sets out four kinds of prophets.

The prophet whose calling concerns only himself. This nabi, unlike a messenger sent to others, is a prophet for himself alone. He is not charged with passing on the signs or divine inspiration (ilham) that he receives. We might call this a form of prophecy that never goes beyond the prophet's own person.

The prophet who encounters the angel in dreams. This nabi receives signs and inspiration, but also sees or hears the angel who brings him knowledge. He does so through spiritual sight or hearing, and only in dreams, not while awake. He, too, has no mission to a particular community. Lot is given as an example: he lived under the guidance of Abraham, who was both his prophet and his Imam, and followed Abraham's sacred law. Muhammad before his first waking vision of the angel bringing revelation is another example. Until then, he was a nabi, but not yet a messenger (rasul).

These first two kinds of prophecy, neither of which involves bringing a new law, are especially important to Shiite thought. We have already learned that what Islam calls walayat—the spiritual initiation associated with God's friends (awliya)—continues, under a different name, a form of prophecy that began with humanity itself. Shiism rests on the conviction that this hidden or inward prophecy (nubuwwat batiniya) will continue until the end of time.

The prophet sent to a community without bringing a new law. This nabi possesses the spiritual gifts of the first two kinds, but has two more: he can see and hear the angel while awake, not merely in dreams, and he is sent to a community, whether large or small. He is a prophet-messenger (nabi mursal). Jonah and, more generally, the prophets of Israel are examples. They brought no new sacred law but followed the law of Moses.

The prophet-messenger who brings a new law. In addition to the spiritual gifts already described, this messenger no longer lives under the law of an earlier prophet. He is sent to reveal a new sacred law to humanity. This is law-giving prophecy (nubuwwat al-tashri'). The Sixth Imam's teaching names five such great prophets. Other lists usually give six, beginning with Adam, or sometimes seven if they include David, whose Psalms are treated in the Qur'an as a separate revealed book. The great periods of law-giving prophecy are then marked by Adam, Noah, Abraham, Moses, David, Jesus, and Muhammad. These are the prophets called ulu'l-'azm: people of unwavering resolve.

Each of these great prophets began as a nabi before becoming a messenger. Their mission matured gradually under divine guidance. During their lives, they were also Imams: spiritual guides. As we will see, Ismaili thought differs on this point.
But Twelver Shiism goes on to explain the qualities an Imam must possess in order to succeed a prophet. It does so through the Qur'anic account of Abraham's appointment as Imam, cited here as 2:118.

Shiite theologians regularly appeal to this verse to defend their understanding of the Imam and answer Sunni objections. God says to Abraham: “I am making you an Imam for the peoples.” Abraham asks, “And from among my descendants?” God replies, “My promise does not include the wrongdoers (al-zalimin)—those who act unjustly.”

Abraham was asking that his descendants should share in the office of Imam. God's reply means that an Imam must possess an inner spiritual purity that physical descent alone can never confer. By insisting that the Twelve Imams of the Prophet's family (ahl al-bayt) possessed this special purity ('isma), Shiites reject the misleading claim repeated by certain Orientalist scholars that their idea of the Imam rests simply on family descent. There have been thousands of imamzadehs, children of Imams, but only twelve Imams.

The Imam therefore requires more than ancestry. He must be expressly designated by the preceding Imam (nass) and possess 'isma. We should not translate this last term simply as infallibility, which has acquired a particular and rather narrow meaning in the West. More accurate words are protection from wrongdoing, freedom from sin, and purity—the qualities suggested by the Greek anamartetos.
This explains the name “the Fourteen Pure Ones” (Chahardeh ma'sum): the Prophet, his daughter Fatima, and the Twelve Imams.

As we have already seen, this Shiite understanding prevents us from treating the line of Twelve Imams as though it were just another ruling dynasty. The spiritual gift of the guardians of the Grail, after all, does not come from the political legitimacy of one dynasty over another. Sunni and Shiite theologians may both use the word Imam, but they mean fundamentally different things by it.

Seen in this light, Mulla Sadra's account of knowledge develops what Ja'far al-Sadiq had already taught about prophecy. The Sixth Imam distinguished the prophets by their capacity for spiritual vision and knowledge of sacred realities. That distinction laid the foundation for a philosophy of prophecy.

We can now use it to understand the Imam's own spiritual rank—and why prophecy, in a sense we must define carefully, can continue to the end of time even though the revelation of new sacred laws has ended.

The Fifth Imam, Muhammad al-Baqir, father of Ja'far al-Sadiq, was asked about a Qur'anic verse (19:55) that calls Ishmael, son of Abraham, a prophet and messenger—the third kind in the scheme above. His answer confirms the earlier teaching:

“A nabi in the simple sense,” he said, “is one who sees visions in dreams and hears the angel's voice, but does not see the angel with his eyes while awake. A messenger (rasul) hears the angel's voice and sees him in dreams, but also sees and hears him while awake. […] The Imam, however, hears the angel's voice in dreams without seeing him.”

Mulla Sadra's very important discussion of this teaching is quoted in the note. The final distinction matters enormously. In the way he receives knowledge, the Imam resembles the nabi of the second kind.
We will soon see what follows from this.

The Eighth Imam, Ali al-Rida (d. 203 AH / 818 CE), repeats the teaching in another reported saying. He also identifies the angel through whom knowledge comes: Gabriel, the Holy Spirit, the Pen. Mulla Sadra then takes the explanation further. He begins with the different names the Qur'an gives Gabriel and shows how they support the identification of Gabriel with the philosophers' Active Intellect.

Gabriel, he explains, “brings divine communication (wahy) to the prophets, inspiration (ilham) to God's friends (awliya)—the Imams who are close to God—and truthful visions in dreams to spiritual seekers.” The degree of spiritual knowledge therefore depends on how the angel appears: seen while one is awake, seen in a dream, or heard without being seen. Since the person who will guide others must first be guided by the angel, we have to be careful not to misunderstand these experiences.

We must use the capacities of spiritual perception to understand, at the level where they are true, Qur'anic passages that speak of Gabriel “descending” (nuzul) into the messenger's heart, or taking human form before him. Mary (Maryam), for example, is said to have seen the angel “take the form of a faultless human being” (19:17)—a form of perfect beauty.

A philosophy of prophecy therefore needs a theory of knowing through images, and of the imaginal world: a world encountered through spiritual imagination, but not dismissed as unreal. Mulla Sadra developed just such a theory with remarkable skill.

He begins by challenging many Islamic philosophers (hukama' islamiyin) and others who claim to speak for philosophy. They regard forms seen in visions, and sounds heard inwardly, as nothing more than impressions on the faculty of imagination (hiss mushtarak). On their view, this faculty is a bodily power located towards the front of the brain, and it disappears when the body dies.

Mulla Sadra argues throughout his work for something very different: imagination is a spiritual power. It does not die with the physical body. It is, in a sense, the soul's subtle body. The opposing view, he says,

comes from a profound lack of knowledge of the world of Malakut—the angelic world of heavenly souls—and from a weakness of faith in the angels, in revelation as it takes form, and in the Book. For these are beings that exist concretely in their own right. They do not need something else in which to exist, as passing qualities do.
Indeed, their existence is much more real than that of outward things. Yet theirs is another world, one that cannot be perceived by our impure senses.

After Mulla Sadra, his whole school continued to stress imagination as a way of knowing, distinct both from the physical senses and from pure intellect. This view of angels and knowledge fits remarkably well—and may even help inspire—a philosophy that says all sensory perception already involves active imagination. What we perceive is not the form of external matter in itself, but the form present within the soul.
Active imagination can turn through the senses towards the outward appearance (zahir) of the visible world.

But appearances in the world of ordinary experience ('alam al-shahadat) can be misleading: what something seems to be may differ from its hidden reality. Things are different when imagination turns towards the world beyond the senses.

When light from the higher world of Malakut reaches the innermost heart (sirr al-qalb), the image that takes shape reveals divine realities as they are. Here the visible form agrees with the inward truth. Its beauty does not deceive. This is true imagination (imaginatio vera).
Mulla Sadra knows that remarkable secrets lie here. The forms appearing in someone's dreams, for example, can reveal the person's hidden reality—the “inner person” (batin).

We have now identified the human capacity through which the angel's action and the different kinds of prophecy meet. Through it, divine communication (wahy) occurs when the angel appears to a messenger while he is awake. Inspiration (ilham) occurs when a nabi who is not a messenger sees or hears the angel in dreams. This makes it easier to understand why Shiite thinkers compare the knowledge given to an ordinary nabi with the knowledge given to an Imam.

Their situations are, in fact, the same in one decisive respect. Both belong among the muhaddathun: “those to whom the angels speak.” A saying frequently attributed to the Prophet declares: “In my community there are people who converse with the angels, people to whom the angels tell things (muhaddathun).” This teaching has enormous consequences for the history of spirituality in Islam, and its full meaning cannot be separated from what the Shiite Imams taught.

Commenting on another teaching of the Fifth Imam, Mulla Sadra explains that those to whom angels speak do not necessarily see an angel face to face, or even in a dream. This angelic conversation (tahdith) takes place within the most deeply hidden region of awareness (fi batin al-sirr). It is spiritual speech (kalam 'aqli), a spiritual account or communication (hadith ruhani). Borrowing the language of Semnani, we could call it a conversation between a spiritual seeker and “the Gabriel of their own being.”

At this point, the philosophy of prophecy reaches its highest expression in the presence of an inner guide. This guide is the source of teaching that is secret or inward in the fullest sense (ta'lim batini): teaching received through spiritual hearing.
We can now see why these Shiite teachings challenge an understanding of Islam that treats religion merely as an inherited law and confines its meaning to the outward words of an earlier revelation.

Among the spiritual states described by the philosophy of prophecy, set aside the special case of seeing Gabriel and hearing him speak while awake, when his words bring a new sacred law. All the remaining states are shared, in various ways, by messengers (rusul), prophets who are not messengers (anbiya), and the muhaddathun, those to whom angels speak—that is, the Imams and God's friends (awliya).

As the Imams say, the earth is never without people who carry divine secrets, even if most human beings do not know who they are. Mulla Sadra explains that hidden, inward prophecy (nubuwwat batiniya) therefore continues until the final Imam appears openly.

What has ended is only the form of prophecy that brings a new sacred law (nubuwwat al-tashri') and, with it, the use of the title nabi. Even the mission of the messenger (risala) and divine communication (wahy) have ceased only in a particular sense, since warnings (indharat) and encouraging signs (mubashshirat) continue.
Muhammad was indeed the Seal of the Prophets. There will be no new nabi.

Yet this other, hidden form of prophecy continues without end. Understood at its source, it is called walayat. These ideas were already present in the teachings of the Shiite Imams at the beginning of Islam.
Yet when placed beside official Islam as it developed historically, they have a truly revolutionary force.
Let us gather these ideas together and draw out what they mean.

First, what makes Muhammad's knowledge distinctive, as the Seal of the Prophets? We need not enter into every detail of the Islamic and Shiite understanding of prophetic inspiration—though a comparison with the different Christian explanations of how scripture is inspired would be valuable. Instead, let us follow Mulla Sadra's comments on the teaching of the Fifth Imam cited earlier. He writes:

The revealed Books—the Books “sent down from heaven” (munazzala)—have reached their completion in one Book, the Qur'an. It is the Word of God (Kalam Allah), through which Truth descends into the heart of His servant. As God Himself says, Gabriel brought down into your heart the Book that confirms the sacred Books before it (2:91).

This means that Gabriel truly brought down into the Prophet's heart the spiritual realities (haqa'iq) of the Qur'an, not merely the outward form of words—words written on tablets and readable by anyone who understands Hebrew or Syriac. No! What he brought down was the inner, spiritual reality (haqiqa), not just the outer form.

What, then, distinguishes the revelations given to the earlier prophets who “brought a Book” from the revelation bestowed upon the Seal of the Prophets? Mulla Sadra explains by bringing together several Qur'anic verses. The spiritual content—the inner reality (haqiqa)—of the Qur'an descended into Muhammad's heart before its outward form of words and letters, before the Word (Kalam) was spoken, and before the heavenly speaker, the angel, appeared to him.

It is this spiritual essence of the Book that the Qur'an calls “a light by which We guide” (42:52). The light of the Word (nur al-Kalam) is this inner reality. And the light that filled the Prophet's heart shines in turn upon those joined to him not merely through outward family descent (munasaba suriya) but also through a spiritual bond (ma'nawiya): the Twelve Imams. Their relationship to Muhammad has both dimensions, spiritual and familial.

The other heavenly Books, by contrast, were brought down to earlier prophets in an outward form, in keeping with the outward aspect of those prophets' missions ('ala zawahiri-him). They were written on tablets or pages that anyone able to read could understand. Both the prophets and their communities were guided by those Books. The Qur'an says, for example, that God “sent down the Torah and the Gospel as guidance for humanity” (3:2).

For Muhammad, the Seal of the Prophets, something different took place. The eternal lights of the Qur'an became present in his heart, and this made him personally the bearer of guidance (hidaya). After him, the Twelve Imams inherited that role. Mulla Sadra puts the difference like this. Each earlier prophet brought his people a Book that served as a light: “The One who sent down the Book Moses brought as light and guidance” (6:91).
But Muhammad's own heart had become light, and with that light came a Book: “A light has come to us from God”—understood here as Muhammad—“and a clear Book”—the Qur'an (5:18).

That is the essential difference. Its source lies in the mystery of the primordial Reality of Muhammad, which we discussed in Chapter Five. In the earlier pattern, a prophet is sent and brings with him the light of a Book. In Muhammad's case, the prophet is himself light, and a Book accompanies him.

For the Muslim understanding of sacred scripture, the Book therefore takes on a unique, final significance through its connection to the Seal of the Prophets. We have just seen what makes Muhammad pre-eminent among the prophets.

In Shiite teachings about divine wisdom, the faith of his community (iman, something deeper than merely outward submission, islam) is, at heart, knowledge of that light. It is not simply agreement with the written words, because the words themselves presuppose the light they express.

This is how the verse is understood: “He has inscribed faith upon their hearts and strengthened them with a Spirit from Himself” (58:22). What faith recognizes in the coming of the final Prophet is the manifestation of the divine Name that gathers all the Names into itself. Muhammad is the earthly manifestation of the glorified Word—the eternal prophetic Reality (Haqiqat Muhammadiya).

Now the question we raised earlier returns of its own accord. The final Prophet has come, but he is no longer here. He revealed a Book whose written words form the outward covering of the light present in his heart. After him, who will keep people from stopping at that outward form? Who will lead them towards the inner reality that gives it light?

There must be a guide whose task is not to reveal another sacred law (sharia), but to uncover the hidden meaning of the law already given. The earth can never be without such a guide, whether everyone knows who he is or he remains hidden. That, as we have seen, is the heart of the Shiite understanding.

The age of prophecy has been followed by the age of walayat, the initiation into inward spiritual knowledge. There are no more nabis, but there are still God's friends (awliya), people who know the hidden truths of faith.

Walayat begins with God's particular love for the Twelve Imams, whom that love sets apart as His friends. Their very persons are manifestations (theophanies) of divine love. Among their followers, walayat is also the devoted love directed towards the Imams as the forms in which God's love appears. By taking part in this loving devotion, their followers, too, can become friends of God (see Chapter Seven below).

The age of walayat is therefore an age of initiation into the ultimate purpose of love and into the secret that inner knowledge discovers beneath the words of prophetic revelation. Such knowledge recognizes those who, at each stage of the spiritual journey (maqam), become the “place where divine revelation appears” (see Chapter Five above). That is why the writers we are studying say that without walayat no faith is acceptable to God.

Walayat opens the hidden meaning of prophecy (batin al-nubuwwa), and God's friends are the guides who lead others into that meaning. More precisely, we have seen that a nabi who is not a messenger possesses a kind of knowledge of sacred realities also shared by the Imams, God's friends, and the muhaddathun, “those to whom the angels speak.” It is therefore accurate to say that one form of prophecy continues under the name walayat.

This is not, and never again will be, the law-giving prophecy of the great messengers. It is inward or esoteric prophecy (nubuwwat batiniya), concerned with realities hidden within the outward forms of religion.

Because that inner prophecy spans the whole history of humanity, we might say that Shiism glimpsed the beginnings of a wider understanding of religions and their histories—one whose centre cannot be an event left behind in the past. This is why Shiite thought looks towards a future disclosure, a horizon associated with the Paraclete, the promised spiritual helper.
We will not be surprised to find the Twelfth Imam identified with the Paraclete by Haydar Amuli and other thinkers.
We have already noted something Shiite writers often say. In the prophetic ages before Muhammad, the term wali—a friend of God, plural awliya—was not used. Such people were called nabis.

Yet what Islam now means by walayat is precisely what earlier ages called prophecy in the sense of nubuwwa without risala: prophecy without a mission to bring a new sacred law. The idea has not changed; only the name has. Muhammad proclaimed himself the Seal of the Prophets (Khatim al-anbiya), and so the word nabi can no longer be used of those who come after him.

Yet the final Prophet's community must still contain the people of whom he said, “There are people who are not prophets, and yet the prophets envy them.” These are the Imams, the friends of God, and those who are friends of those friends. When Muhammad said, “There will be no prophet after me,” he meant that law-giving prophecy had come to an end. There would be no new law, no new revelation of a sharia.

But we have also learned that, with the Prophet no longer present, the Qur'an on its own cannot serve as the living witness and answerer. Its words hold hidden meanings that cannot simply be learned from outside. They are handed on by those who possess inspired knowledge (ilham). This is why inward prophecy (nubuwwat batiniya) must continue until the end of time.

It is the prophecy of the Witnesses. Their unbroken succession will lead to the Resurrection (Qiyama) that ends our present aeon—our age of the world. Then the one who has until now been the unseen guide of all these Witnesses will at last appear openly: the Twelfth Imam.

When our writers repeatedly say that prophecy (nobowwat) is temporary while walayat is eternal, they mean two different things. What comes to an end is the kind of prophecy that brings a divine law (nobowwat al-tashri). What continues forever is walayat: the spiritual bond with God that belongs to God's friends and guides. In this sense, it is an eternal form of prophecy, and its religion is the eternal religion of spiritual humanity.
We know that walayat is also a central idea throughout Sufism.

But now that we have brought its specifically Shiite meaning back into view, an important question arises. Can we go on discussing walayat in Sufism without mentioning its Shiite origins? Worse still, can we ignore the fundamental place it holds in Shiite theology? Its meaning could hardly be further from the religion of outward legal requirements that characterizes orthodox Sunni teaching. In the past, even the suspicion that someone was secretly Shiite could have terrible consequences.

Consider the trial of Suhrawardi, who died in Aleppo in 587 AH (1191 CE). The crucial question put to him was: “Have you claimed in your books that God can create a prophet whenever He wishes?” The accusation really concerned the opening of his great work, The Philosophy of Illumination (Hikmat al-Ishraq), where he maintains that there must always be a Qotb, a spiritual “pole” without whom the Earth could not exist.

We now understand what that claim involves. Suhrawardi tried to defend himself by asking whether God was inherently incapable of creating another prophet. But that question alone was enough to bring a declaration of unbelief (takfir) and his condemnation (see Book II below).

So far, we have examined the relationship between the Prophet and the Imam in terms of knowledge. After the prophet who brought the divine law, there still had to be guides with the special gift of leading people into the inner meaning of prophetic revelation. The usual definition is that walayat is the inner dimension of prophecy (batin al-nobowwat).

But if the Prophet represents the outward side and the Imam the inward side of one reality, their connection must go deeper than their roles in earthly history. It must be rooted in the very nature of spiritual reality. The idea of prophetic inheritance—the Prophet's spiritual heirs—expresses, here on Earth, the structure of an eternal prophetic reality: the Muhammadan Reality (Haqiqat mohammadiya). We have already considered this reality at different levels of the spiritual universe. Now we must look at it in relation to the Prophet's mission in this world.

Here I shall follow mainly Haydar Amoli, a fourteenth-century thinker we have often met already. He is especially skilled at drawing out the meaning of the sayings handed down from his Imams, while staying faithful to them (see Book IV, Chapter 1 below). When we speak of a prophetic religion or a prophetic philosophy, we naturally assume that prophecy exists. Earlier (p. 235), we explained what the word itself means. It has nothing to do, in the first instance, with “predicting the future.”

But if prophecy is what guides humanity on Earth, and if that guidance has always been necessary, when did prophecy begin? We should not expect an answer based on a dateable event in ordinary history.

But neither should we expect merely a myth. As we have seen, these thinkers recognize events belonging to a realm beyond recorded history, which we have called metahistory. For them, prophecy really begins there: in Heaven, before human beings existed on Earth (see Chapter V above). Versions of this idea appear in both Twelver Shiite and Ismaili spiritual thought. The first prophet was the being known by various names as the Heavenly Human, or Anthropos.
The different kinds of prophet described by the Shiite Imams correspond to distinctions that Haydar Amoli also draws. Shiite authors distinguish two things when they speak of prophecy (nobowwat).

First, there is prophecy that teaches (nobowwat al-ta'rif). We might call it “gnostic” prophecy, because what it teaches is direct spiritual knowledge (ma'rifat) of God's Essence, Names, and Attributes. It includes the first three kinds of prophet in the scheme discussed earlier (p. 238): the 124,000 prophets mentioned in tradition, whose missions together cover the whole history of religions.

Second, there is prophecy that establishes a law (nobowwat al-tashri). In addition to teaching spiritual truth, it brings a sharia, a divine law. This is the fourth kind of prophet in that earlier scheme.

Prophecy also has two dimensions: one absolute and universal (motlaq, 'amm), the other limited, relative, and particular (mogayyad, khass). The particular dimension appears in each individual prophet. Each is a visible manifestation (mazhar) of the eternal reality of prophecy. But only the Seal of the Prophets manifests prophecy in its absolute, universal form.

To understand this, we have to look back to prophecy's very beginning, to the primordial Muhammadan Reality discussed in Chapter V. We must consider the Prophet's reality as something that existed before time. This is the meaning of the paradoxical saying: “I was already a prophet when Adam was still between water and clay”—that is, before Adam had even taken shape. These words refer to a primordial, ideal prophecy (nobowwat haqiqiya), which begins before time and continues from age to age (nobowwat azaliya baqiya).
